History

The herb grinder as a two-half cylindrical shredder is documented in the early 1900s, with William Wingfield and John Balding of Boort, Victoria, Australia patenting a novel grinding device in 1905, and the form was popularised in the 1960s as cannabis use spread. Early grinders were simple wood or metal cylinders; the modern four-piece aluminium grinder with a kief screen is a later refinement of that same two-half idea. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Museums, trade guides, and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change, and the sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The the manual herb grinder works by two interlocking halves with opposing diamond-shaped teeth; twisting the halves in opposite directions shears dried herb caught between the teeth. It is made from anodised aluminium body, stainless-steel teeth, stainless-steel mesh screen, neodymium magnet lid closure, and a common example measures 63 mm diameter, 48 mm tall in four pieces, grinding chamber 28 mm deep. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Anodised aluminium (6061) body; stainless-steel teeth; stainless-steel 100-micron mesh screen; neodymium magnet in lid

Dimensions: 63 mm diameter x 48 mm tall; grinding chamber 28 mm deep; 4 pieces

Mechanism: Two halves with opposing diamond teeth; hand-twisted in opposite directions; ground herb falls through holes into a storage chamber; fine particles pass the mesh into a kief chamber

Use: Break dried herb into pea-sized pieces, place between the teeth, replace the lid, twist 10 to 15 times until the halves turn freely, then collect ground herb from the storage chamber

Care: Brush out residue after use; wash aluminium parts in warm soapy water, dry fully; clean the mesh screen with a soft brush; keep the magnet faces free of metal dust

Variants: 2-piece (grind only); 3-piece (grind plus storage); 4-piece (grind, storage, and kief screen); wood, plastic, zinc, aluminium, and stainless-steel versions

Science proof

Shear, not crushing, is the working principle. Opposing diamond teeth pass each other with a small clearance, and the edges cut dried flower along its natural fracture planes. Aluminium 6061 is chosen because it is light, machines cleanly, and its anodised surface resists corrosion from plant resins. The teeth stay sharp because the load is spread across 49 teeth and each tooth meets only a small piece of herb at a time. Ground particles fall through sized holes in the grinding plate by gravity once they are smaller than the hole diameter, which is why a dozen steady turns produces a fairly uniform particle size instead of powder. The 100-micron mesh in a four-piece grinder is a sieve: particles finer than 100 microns, including the small resin glands called trichomes, pass through, while larger ground herb stays above. Friction is low because the herb is dry and brittle, and the magnet lid keeps the halves aligned so the teeth never clash metal on metal. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.

Math proof

The demo computes the grinding chamber as a cylinder. With diameter 63.0 mm the radius is 31.5 mm, so the chamber volume is pi times radius squared times the chamber depth of 28.0 mm, which the program reports in cubic millimetres and cubic centimetres. The screen area uses the same circle formula with the screen diameter of 56.0 mm. Dividing the tooth count of 49 by the chamber floor area gives teeth per square centimetre, a check that the teeth are spread evenly rather than crowded. Each of the 12 turns in the worked example moves the teeth past each other once, so the total cutting passes are the tooth count times the turns, and the program prints the volume and area so the reader can repeat the arithmetic with a pocket calculator. The formulas are shown in full, the numbers come from the specification in this record, and the demo prints both runs with SHA-256 digests so the reader can confirm the computation is deterministic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation.

Use and care

Break dried herb into pea-sized pieces, place between the teeth, replace the lid, twist 10 to 15 times until the halves turn freely, then collect ground herb from the storage chamber Brush out residue after use; wash aluminium parts in warm soapy water, dry fully; clean the mesh screen with a soft brush; keep the magnet faces free of metal dust Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts such as screens, balloons, or filter tips when they no longer do their job. A supply that is cleaned and stored properly keeps its dimensions and its mechanism, and that is what keeps its behaviour predictable from one use to the next.

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

  • Weedmaps — Grinder definition — https://weedmaps.com/learn/dictionary/grinder — A grinder breaks cannabis flower into smaller pieces for joints, blunts, and bowls; place material between the teeth and twist the top and bottom in opposite directions; herb grinders may include a kief catcher in the bottom chamber.

"""Demo: manual grinder chamber volume — The Manual Herb Grinder."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    d = 63.0; h = 28.0; teeth = 49; screen_d = 56.0; turns = 12
    r = d / 2.0
    chamber_mm3 = math.pi * r * r * h
    chamber_cm3 = chamber_mm3 / 1000.0
    screen_area_mm2 = math.pi * (screen_d / 2.0) ** 2
    teeth_per_cm2 = teeth / (math.pi * r * r / 100.0)
    return {"chamber_volume_mm3": round(chamber_mm3, 2), "chamber_volume_cm3": round(chamber_cm3, 2), "screen_area_mm2": round(screen_area_mm2, 2), "teeth": teeth, "turns": turns, "teeth_per_cm2": round(teeth_per_cm2, 2)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["chamber_volume_mm3", "chamber_volume_cm3", "screen_area_mm2", "teeth", "turns", "teeth_per_cm2"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

History

Electric grinders grew out of the manual grinder once small rechargeable lithium-ion batteries and compact motors became cheap. Early battery grinders were little more than a motor bolted to a manual tooth plate; later designs added sensors, as in the banana bros OTTO, whose manual describes SMART Milling Technology that senses the material and adjusts direction, speed, and pressure. USB-C charging replaced disposable batteries on most portable models, and transparent chambers let the user watch particle size as it changes. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Museums, trade guides, and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change, and the sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The the electric herb grinder works by a rechargeable lithium-ion battery drives a small electric motor that spins blades, teeth, or a milling plate inside a closed chamber. It is made from abs or aluminium housing, stainless-steel blades or milling plate, lithium-ion battery, usb-c charging port, and a common example measures 110 mm tall, 55 mm diameter, chamber holds up to 3 g per load. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: ABS or aluminium housing; stainless-steel blades or milling plate; lithium-ion rechargeable battery; USB-C port

Dimensions: 110 mm tall x 55 mm diameter; grinding chamber holds up to 3 g per load

Mechanism: Battery-powered motor spins blades or a milling plate; some models sense load and reverse or change speed; grind time controls fineness, about 2 seconds coarse, 4 seconds medium, 6 seconds finer

Use: Charge fully, load dried herb without overfilling, close the chamber, press and hold the button for the chosen time, then open and collect the ground herb

Care: Empty the chamber after use; brush blades clean; wipe the housing; recharge before storage; do not immerse the motor housing in water

Variants: Blade grinders; burr and milling-plate grinders; mill-and-fill models that drop ground herb into a cone; replaceable-battery and USB-C rechargeable models

Science proof

An electric grinder converts stored chemical energy into rotational kinetic energy. The lithium-ion cell holds charge as ions shuttle between electrodes; on discharge it delivers about 3.7 volts, and the motor turns that electrical power into torque on the blade shaft. Power equals voltage times current, so a 5-watt motor at 3.7 volts draws about 1.35 amps while running. The blades cut by the same shear action as a manual grinder, but the motor supplies many more cutting passes per second, which is why a load is ground in seconds rather than a dozen hand turns. Short bursts matter: running the motor too long adds friction heat and can turn herb toward powder. The battery capacity in milliamp-hours converts to watt-hours by multiplying volts by amp-hours, and dividing that stored energy by the energy of one grind gives the number of grinds per charge. USB-C charging simply refills the same cell through a standard 5-volt supply. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.

Math proof

The demo starts from the battery: 3.7 volts times 2000.0 milliamp-hours divided by 1000 gives the stored energy in watt-hours. One grind costs motor power times time: 5.0 watts times 6.0 seconds is 30.0 joules, which divided by 3600 gives watt-hours per grind. Dividing the stored watt-hours by the watt-hours per grind gives the number of grinds per charge, and dividing motor power by voltage gives the motor current in amps. All of these numbers come from the specification in this record, and the program prints each one with its unit so the reader can check the arithmetic step by step. The demo runs the computation twice and prints SHA-256 digests of both runs, so the reader can confirm the result is deterministic and not a one-off printout. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation.

Charge fully, load dried herb without overfilling, close the chamber, press and hold the button for the chosen time, then open and collect the ground herb Empty the chamber after use; brush blades clean; wipe the housing; recharge before storage; do not immerse the motor housing in water Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts such as screens, balloons, or filter tips when they no longer do their job. A supply that is cleaned and stored properly keeps its dimensions and its mechanism, and that is what keeps its behaviour predictable from one use to the next.

"""Demo: electric grinder battery energy — The Electric Herb Grinder."""
import hashlib
def compute():
    v = 3.7; cap_mah = 2000.0; motor_w = 5.0; grind_s = 6.0; load_g = 3.0
    battery_wh = v * (cap_mah / 1000.0)
    energy_per_grind_wh = motor_w * grind_s / 3600.0
    energy_per_grind_j = motor_w * grind_s
    grinds_per_charge = battery_wh / energy_per_grind_wh
    current_a = motor_w / v
    return {"battery_wh": round(battery_wh, 3), "energy_per_grind_Wh": round(energy_per_grind_wh, 5), "energy_per_grind_J": round(energy_per_grind_j, 2), "grinds_per_charge": round(grinds_per_charge, 1), "motor_current_A": round(current_a, 2), "load_g": load_g}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["battery_wh", "energy_per_grind_Wh", "energy_per_grind_J", "grinds_per_charge", "motor_current_A", "load_g"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Electric grinders grew out of the manual grinder once small rechargeable lithium-ion batteries and compact motors became cheap. Early battery grinders were little more than a motor bolted to a manual tooth plate; later designs added sensors, as in the banana bros OTTO, whose manual describes SMART Milling Technology that senses the material and adjusts direction, speed, and pressure. USB-C charging replaced disposable batteries on most portable models, and transparent chambers let the user watch particle size as it changes. In everyday use it is a simple, mechanical object with no electronics in the manual form and no hidden parts: what you see is what does the work, and its behaviour can be checked by measuring its parts and doing the arithmetic in this record. This record gives the full public account: its history, how it works in detail, a complete specification, the physics behind it, worked mathematics tied to its own dimensions, and a runnable program that computes its key volumes, areas, and energies. It makes no medical claim and gives no dosage advice; it describes a supply, its materials, and its mechanism, and it cites real public sources for every fact it states. Laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction, so readers should check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply. The record is part of the public edition of the marijuana supplies database, paired with a Signature design-study edition of the same supply.

History

Portable dry-herb vaporizers descend from desktop convection machines such as the Volcano, miniaturised once lithium-ion batteries and precise temperature controllers became small enough to carry. Early portables used simple conduction ovens with preset temperatures; later models added hybrid conduction-convection heating, digital displays, and phone apps. The PAX line is a well-known example of the pocket form: a slim metal body, a small oven, and a mouthpiece, with heat modes stepped from about 374 F to 428 F. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Museums, trade guides, and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change, and the sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The the portable dry-herb vaporizer works by a battery-powered heater warms a small oven holding ground herb to a set temperature below combustion, and the user draws the released vapour through a mouthpiece. It is made from anodised aluminium or stainless-steel body, ceramic or stainless-steel oven, lithium-ion battery, glass or plastic mouthpiece, and a common example measures 100 mm tall, 30 mm wide, oven holds about 0.25 g. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Anodised aluminium or stainless-steel body; ceramic or stainless-steel oven; lithium-ion battery; glass or plastic mouthpiece

Dimensions: 100 mm tall x 30 mm wide x 22 mm deep; oven holds about 0.25 g of ground herb

Mechanism: Conduction, convection, or hybrid heating; temperature set by presets or a digital control, typically 160 C to 220 C (320 F to 428 F); heat-up in 10 to 90 seconds depending on method

Use: Grind herb medium-fine, fill the oven loosely, set the temperature, wait for the ready signal, then draw slowly through the mouthpiece

Care: Empty the oven after it cools; brush out residue; clean the mouthpiece and oven with isopropyl alcohol on a cotton swab when cool; recharge the battery

Variants: Conduction-only pocket vapes; convection portables; hybrid models such as the Mighty+ and Crafty+; one-button preset models and full digital-control models

Science proof

A vaporizer works by phase change without combustion. Heating dried herb raises the temperature of its volatile compounds until they boil off as vapour, while the plant fibre itself stays below its burning point, which sources place above about 230 C. Conduction transfers heat by direct contact between the hot oven wall and the herb, which is fast but can heat unevenly. Convection carries heat in a stream of hot air that passes through the herb, which is slower to start but more even. Hybrid ovens use both. The energy needed is the sensible heat of the herb plus the sensible heat of the oven metal or ceramic: mass times specific heat capacity times temperature rise. A lithium-ion battery stores that energy chemically and releases it as electrical heat through a resistive heater, and a controller cycles the heater on and off to hold the set temperature. Lower set temperatures release lighter, more fragrant compounds first; higher set temperatures release more of the heavier compounds. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.

Math proof

The demo uses the sensible-heat formula Q equals m times c times the temperature rise. The herb mass is 0.25 g, its specific heat capacity is 1.7 joules per gram per degree Celsius, and the rise from 20.0 C to 190.0 C is 170.0 degrees, so the herb heat is the product of those three numbers. The oven is heated as well: 12.0 g of oven material at 0.9 joules per gram per degree over the same rise. Adding the two heats gives the total heat per session in joules, and dividing by 3600 converts it to watt-hours. Dividing the battery energy of 10.0 watt-hours by the watt-hours per session gives the number of sessions per charge. The program prints every step, runs the computation twice, and prints SHA-256 digests so the reader can verify the result is deterministic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation.

Use and care

Grind herb medium-fine, fill the oven loosely, set the temperature, wait for the ready signal, then draw slowly through the mouthpiece Empty the oven after it cools; brush out residue; clean the mouthpiece and oven with isopropyl alcohol on a cotton swab when cool; recharge the battery Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts such as screens, balloons, or filter tips when they no longer do their job. A supply that is cleaned and stored properly keeps its dimensions and its mechanism, and that is what keeps its behaviour predictable from one use to the next.

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

Sources

  • Herb.co — How does a dry herb vaporizer work — https://herb.co/guides/how-does-dry-herb-vaporizer-work-vaping-vs-smoking — A dry herb vaporizer heats ground flower to a set temperature below its burning point so cannabinoids and terpenes are released as vapor; plant material starts to burn above about 230 C (446 F); most dry herb vapes work roughly 160 C to 220 C (320 F to 428 F).
  • Vape Observation — What is a dry herb vaporizer — https://vapeobservation.com/what-is-a-dry-herb-vaporizers-a-comprehensive-guide/ — A dry herb vaporizer heats dried plant material to a precise temperature, releasing active compounds as vapor without reaching combustion; combustion happens around 450 F (232 C); typical operating range is 315 F to 430 F (157 C to 221 C); conduction, convection, and hybrid heating are the three main methods.

"""Demo: portable vaporizer heating energy — The Portable Dry-Herb Vaporizer."""
import hashlib
def compute():
    herb_g = 0.25; t0 = 20.0; t1 = 190.0; cp = 1.7; battery_wh = 10.0; oven_g = 12.0; oven_cp = 0.9
    q_herb_j = herb_g * cp * (t1 - t0)
    q_oven_j = oven_g * oven_cp * (t1 - t0)
    q_total_j = q_herb_j + q_oven_j
    q_total_wh = q_total_j / 3600.0
    sessions = battery_wh / q_total_wh
    temp_rise_c = t1 - t0
    return {"herb_heat_J": round(q_herb_j, 2), "oven_heat_J": round(q_oven_j, 2), "total_heat_J": round(q_total_j, 2), "total_heat_Wh": round(q_total_wh, 4), "sessions_per_charge": round(sessions, 1), "temp_rise_C": temp_rise_c}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["herb_heat_J", "oven_heat_J", "total_heat_J", "total_heat_Wh", "sessions_per_charge", "temp_rise_C"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

History

The desktop vaporizer was defined by the Storz & Bickel Volcano, introduced in 2000 and the benchmark for the category ever since. The Volcano Classic is a purely electromechanical machine: an analog dial, a heater, and an air pump, with no screen or app. It filled a detachable balloon, called a bag, with vapour, and the vapour stayed fresh in the balloon for up to 8 hours according to the maker. The later Volcano Hybrid added a digital display, faster heat-up, app and Bluetooth control, and a whip tube for direct draw alongside the balloon. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Museums, trade guides, and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change, and the sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The the desktop vaporizer works by mains power heats air in a large aluminium heat exchanger, and an air pump pushes that hot air through a filling chamber of ground herb into a detachable balloon, or through a whip tube. It is made from aluminium heat exchanger, stainless-steel filling chamber, food-grade balloon material, mains-powered heater and air pump, and a common example measures about 200 mm tall, 200 mm diameter base, 100 w heater, balloon about 3 litres when filled. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Aluminium heat exchanger; stainless-steel filling chamber and screens; food-grade balloon material; mains-powered heater and air pump

Dimensions: About 200 mm tall x 200 mm diameter base; 100 W convection heater; Easy Valve balloon holds about 3 litres when filled

Mechanism: Pure convection in the Classic: heated air passes through the herb and carries vapour into the balloon; the Hybrid adds conduction and a whip; temperature range 130 C to 230 C (266 F to 446 F) on nine dial levels

Use: Grind medium-fine, fill the chamber loosely, preheat until the temperature settles, attach the balloon, run the fan until the balloon is firm, detach it, and inhale through the valve mouthpiece

Care: Empty the chamber after use; replace balloons when worn; clean the filling chamber and screens; wipe the housing; keep the air intake clear

Variants: Volcano Classic (analog dial, balloon only); Volcano Hybrid (digital display, balloon plus whip, app control); other desktop whip and balloon models

Science proof

A desktop vaporizer is a forced-air convection system. Mains electricity heats a large aluminium block, the heat exchanger, which stores thermal energy and holds a steady temperature while air passes over it. The air pump drives room air through that block, so the air leaves at the set temperature, then flows through the filling chamber where it gives up heat to the herb and picks up vapour. Because the herb never touches the heater, the temperature the herb sees is the temperature of the air, which is why the result repeats from session to session. The balloon is a simple reservoir: vapour collects in it, cools slightly as it waits, and the valve mouthpiece releases vapour only when the user draws. Filling volume is airflow rate times fill time, and the heater energy is power times time. The large heat exchanger is the reason a desktop unit holds temperature better than a small portable: its thermal mass resists the cooling effect of each draw of air. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.

Math proof

The demo uses two simple products. First, heat-up energy is heater power times time: 100.0 watts times 180.0 seconds, which the program reports in joules and in watt-hours after dividing by 3600. Second, the filled balloon volume is airflow times fill time: 4.0 litres per minute times 45.0 seconds divided by 60 gives the filled volume in litres, and dividing that by the balloon volume of 3.0 litres gives the fill fraction. Both numbers come from the specification in this record, and the program prints them with units so the reader can repeat the arithmetic by hand. The computation is run twice and the SHA-256 digests of both runs are printed, confirming the result is deterministic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation.

Use and care

Grind medium-fine, fill the chamber loosely, preheat until the temperature settles, attach the balloon, run the fan until the balloon is firm, detach it, and inhale through the valve mouthpiece Empty the chamber after use; replace balloons when worn; clean the filling chamber and screens; wipe the housing; keep the air intake clear Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts such as screens, balloons, or filter tips when they no longer do their job. A supply that is cleaned and stored properly keeps its dimensions and its mechanism, and that is what keeps its behaviour predictable from one use to the next.

if __name__ == "__main__":

History

The bong descends from the hookah and from bamboo water pipes of Asia; the word itself is adapted from the Thai word baung, meaning a wooden cylinder or pipe cut from bamboo. Glass bongs became common in the twentieth century as borosilicate glass made a heat-resistant, clean-tasting water chamber practical. A 1981 United States patent (4,253,475) describes the classic form in detail: a single vertical pipe about 1.5 inches in diameter sealed at the bottom, a bowl on a tube leading in near the bottom, water just above the junction, and a small hole above the water line to clear the chamber. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Museums, trade guides, and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change, and the sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The the water pipe (bong) works by smoke from the bowl travels down a stem below the water line, bubbles up through the water, collects in the chamber, and is drawn to the mouth when the carb is opened or the stem is lifted. It is made from borosilicate glass tube and base, glass downstem and bowl, water as the filtration medium, and a common example measures about 300 mm tall, tube 50 mm diameter, water depth about 50 mm in the base. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Borosilicate glass tube, base, downstem, and bowl; plain water as the filtration medium; optional ice catcher and percolator

Dimensions: About 300 mm tall; tube 50 mm in diameter; base holds water about 50 mm deep; downstem reaches about 25 mm below the water surface

Mechanism: Negative pressure from the draw pulls smoke down the downstem and out below the water line; smoke bubbles up through the water, which cools it and traps heavier particles and some water-soluble molecules; the chamber above the water stores smoke until the carb is opened

Use: Add water so the downstem sits below the surface, pack the bowl, cover the carb, light while drawing slowly until the chamber fills, then open the carb and inhale

Care: Change the water after each session; rinse the base; clean glass with isopropyl alcohol and salt; dry fully; replace a cracked downstem

Variants: Straight tube; beaker base; percolator models with extra diffusion slits; ice-catcher models; multi-chamber models

Science proof

A bong is a gas-washing bottle. Smoke is a mixture of hot gases and small solid particles, and bubbling it through water does two things at once. First, the water is a heat sink: smoke leaving the bowl is hot, and contact with water at room temperature transfers heat out of the gas, so the smoke that reaches the mouth is cooler. Second, the water is a trap: heavier particles such as ash have too much inertia to follow the gas around a bubble wall and strike the water, and some water-soluble molecules dissolve. Smaller bubbles work better because surface area grows as bubble size shrinks: for the same volume of gas, many small bubbles expose far more gas-water interface than a few large ones, which is why diffused downstems and percolators with many small slits are used. The chamber above the water is a reservoir, and the water level sets the pressure the user must overcome: the draw must lift the water column by the depth of the downstem below the surface, a small hydrostatic pressure of water density times gravity times depth. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.

Math proof

The demo treats the tube as a cylinder. The cross-sectional area is pi times the tube radius squared, with a tube diameter of 50.0 mm. Multiplying that area by the water depth of 50.0 mm gives the water volume, and multiplying it by the height above the water gives the chamber volume, both reported in millilitres. A single bubble is treated as a sphere with diameter 4.0 mm: its volume is four thirds pi times radius cubed, and its surface area is four pi times radius squared. The draw pressure is water density times gravity times depth, which the program reports in pascals. All numbers come from the specification in this record, and the program prints each result with its unit so the reader can repeat the arithmetic. It runs the computation twice and prints SHA-256 digests of both runs. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation.

Use and care

Add water so the downstem sits below the surface, pack the bowl, cover the carb, light while drawing slowly until the chamber fills, then open the carb and inhale Change the water after each session; rinse the base; clean glass with isopropyl alcohol and salt; dry fully; replace a cracked downstem Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts such as screens, balloons, or filter tips when they no longer do their job. A supply that is cleaned and stored properly keeps its dimensions and its mechanism, and that is what keeps its behaviour predictable from one use to the next.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (water pipe water and chamber volumes),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py

import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for The Water Pipe (Bong)."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        tube_d = 50.0; height = 300.0; water_h = 50.0; down_d = 12.0; bubble_d = 4.0
        area_mm2 = math.pi * (tube_d / 2.0) ** 2
        water_mm3 = area_mm2 * water_h
        chamber_h = height - water_h
        chamber_mm3 = area_mm2 * chamber_h
        bubble_r = bubble_d / 2.0
        bubble_vol_mm3 = (4.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * bubble_r ** 3

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""

science_proof: A bong is a gas-washing bottle. Smoke is a mixture of hot gases and small solid particles, and bubbling it through water does two things at once. First, the water is a heat sink: smoke leaving the bowl is hot, and contact with water at room temperature transfers heat out of the gas, so the smoke that reaches the mouth is cooler. Second, the water is a trap: heavier particles such as ash have too much inertia to follow the gas around a bubble wall and strike the water, and some water-soluble molecules dissolve. Smaller bubbles work better because surface area grows as bubble size shrinks: for the same volume of gas, many small bubbles expose far more gas-water interface than a few large ones, which is why diffused downstems and percolators with many small slits are used. The chamber above the water is a reservoir, and the water level sets the pressure the user must overcome: the draw must lift the water column by the depth of the downstem below the surface, a small hydrostatic pressure of water density times gravity times depth. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. History

Rolling papers began in Alcoy, Spain, in the 1500s, where smokers wrapped salvaged cigar tobacco in paper scraps; dedicated paper factories followed in the town in the mid-1700s, and a Spanish monk is credited with the first folded booklet around 1765. The trade spread through France and Spain in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries: Zig-Zag traces its origins to France in 1879, introduced interleaved booklets in 1894, and trademarked the name in 1906. RAW launched its first unbleached papers in 2005. Papers were first made for tobacco; cannabis smokers adopted the same sheets, and makers later offered hemp, rice, and flax papers aimed at them. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Museums, trade guides, and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change, and the sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The rolling papers works by a thin sheet of plant-fibre paper with a gum strip along one edge is wrapped around ground herb, sealed by moistening the gum, and the resulting cylinder is lit at one end and drawn from the other. It is made from hemp, rice, flax, or wood-pulp paper, 10 to 14 gsm, with a gum arabic adhesive strip, and a common example measures 1 1/4 size 78 mm x 44 mm; king size 110 mm x 44 mm; booklets of 32 leaves are common. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Hemp, rice, flax, or wood-pulp paper at about 10 to 14 grams per square metre; gum arabic adhesive strip along one long edge

Dimensions: Single wide 70 mm x 36 mm; 1 1/4 size 78 mm x 44 mm; 1 1/2 size 78 mm x 60 mm; King size 110 mm x 44 mm; King slim 110 mm x 53 mm

Mechanism: Ground herb is spread along the paper, the paper is rolled into a cylinder, the gum strip is moistened and pressed to seal the seam, and the finished roll is lit at the tip and drawn from the filter end

Use: Place a filter tip at one end, spread ground herb evenly, roll the paper into a cylinder, lick the gum strip, seal the seam, and twist the open tip closed

Care: Keep booklets dry and flat; store away from damp; use papers before the gum strip dries out or picks up dust

Variants: Hemp, rice, flax, wood-pulp, and clear cellulose papers; bleached white and unbleached brown; flavoured papers; rolls of 3 to 5 metres for custom lengths

Science proof

Rolling paper is a thin, porous sheet of plant fibre, and its behaviour is set by three material facts. First, basis weight, measured in grams per square metre, sets thickness and stiffness: at 10 to 14 grams per square metre the sheet is thin enough to roll tightly yet strong enough not to tear. Second, the fibres are cellulose, and cellulose burns by pyrolysis followed by oxidation, releasing heat that sustains a slow, even burn along the cylinder. Third, the gum strip is gum arabic, a plant polysaccharide that dissolves in water and re-forms a bond as it dries, which is why a licked seam seals without heat. Rice papers are very thin and burn slowly because their dense fibre mat limits airflow; hemp papers are slightly thicker and more structured, which many rollers find easier to handle. The area of one sheet is length times width, and the area of a whole booklet is that area times the leaf count, so a 32-leaf booklet of 1 1/4 papers carries a little over a tenth of a square metre of paper in total. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.

Math proof

The demo starts with one sheet: length times width, 78.0 mm times 44.0 mm, gives the sheet area in square millimetres, and dividing by 100 gives square centimetres. Multiplying the sheet area by 32 leaves gives the booklet area, and dividing by one million converts square millimetres to square metres. Multiplying that area by the basis weight of 12.0 grams per square metre gives the mass of paper in one booklet. The gum strip area is the paper length times the gum width of 4.0 mm. Every number comes from the specification in this record, the program prints each result with its unit, and it runs the computation twice with SHA-256 digests so the reader can confirm the result is deterministic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation.

Use and care

Place a filter tip at one end, spread ground herb evenly, roll the paper into a cylinder, lick the gum strip, seal the seam, and twist the open tip closed Keep booklets dry and flat; store away from damp; use papers before the gum strip dries out or picks up dust Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts such as screens, balloons, or filter tips when they no longer do their job. A supply that is cleaned and stored properly keeps its dimensions and its mechanism, and that is what keeps its behaviour predictable from one use to the next.

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

  • Speakeasy Vaporium — Rolling Papers Guide: Sizes, Materials, and How to Choose — https://speakeasyvaporium.com/blog/rolling-papers-guide/ — Rolling papers are sold in standard sizes named mostly by tradition: Single wide 68-70mm x 34-38mm, 1 1/4 size 76-78mm x 44-48mm, 1 1/2 size 76-78mm x 60-62mm, King size slim 105-110mm x 42-46mm, King size 100-110mm x 55-60mm; materials include wood pulp, rice, hemp, flax, and cellulose; Zig-Zag traces its origins to France in 1879.

First, basis weight, measured in grams per square metre, sets thickness and stiffness: at 10 to 14 grams per square metre the sheet is thin enough to roll tightly yet strong enough not to tear. Second, the fibres are cellulose, and cellulose burns by pyrolysis followed by oxidation, releasing heat that sustains a slow, even burn along the cylinder. Third, the gum strip is gum arabic, a plant polysaccharide that dissolves in water and re-forms a bond as it dries, which is why a licked seam seals without heat. Rice papers are very thin and burn slowly because their dense fibre mat limits airflow; hemp papers are slightly thicker and more structured, which many rollers find easier to handle. The area of one sheet is length times width, and the area of a whole booklet is that area times the leaf count, so a 32-leaf booklet of 1 1/4 papers carries a little over a tenth of a square metre of paper in total. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. body:
History

Pre-rolled cones are the factory answer to hand rolling: the paper is cut, shaped, and tipped before it reaches the user, so filling replaces rolling. Cone making grew with the pre-roll trade, where production runs in four steps described by trade guides: grind the flower to a consistent 1 to 2 mm, sift out stems and sharp material, fill pre-rolled cones by hand or by machine, then close and weigh each unit. Machines such as the Futurola Knockbox can fill many cones in a single cycle. Common cone sizes settled at Standard 84 mm, Classic 98 mm, and King Size 109 mm, with a rolled paper filter tip, called a crutch or roach, already fitted at the narrow end. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Museums, trade guides, and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change, and the sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The pre-rolled cones works by a paper sheet cut as a trapezoid is rolled around a form into a tapered tube with a filter tip at the narrow end; the user fills the wide end, packs the contents, and twists the tip closed. It is made from hemp, rice, or wood-pulp paper, gum arabic seam, rolled paper filter tip 24 mm long, and a common example measures 1 1/4 cone 84 mm long, king cone 109 mm long, filter tip 24 mm. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Hemp, rice, or wood-pulp paper; gum arabic seam; rolled paper or cardboard filter tip, usually 24 mm long

Dimensions: Mini 70 mm; Small / 1 1/4 size 84 mm; Classic 98 mm; King Size 109 mm; filter tip 24 mm; a 1 1/4 cone holds about 0.75 g

Mechanism: Trapezoid-cut paper is rolled into a tapered tube around a form; the filter tip at the narrow end supports the cone, keeps material out of the mouth, and sets the airflow; the wide end is filled, packed, and twisted closed

Use: Hold the cone upright with the filter end down, add ground herb in small amounts, tap to settle, leave about 5 mm at the top, pack gently, and twist the tip closed

Care: Keep cones dry and upright; store in their pack so they are not crushed; check the filter tip is firmly attached before filling

Variants: Mini 70 mm; 1 1/4 size 84 mm; Classic 98 mm; King Size 109 mm; mega 305 mm; hemp, rice, and wood-pulp papers; glass-tip and charcoal-tip versions

Science proof

A cone is a frustum, a cone with its tip cut off, and its shape does real work. The wide end holds more material than the narrow end, so the contents pack more densely toward the filter and more loosely at the tip, which helps the roll burn evenly from the wide end down. The filter tip, or crutch, is a rolled cylinder of paper: it holds the cone open, stops loose material from reaching the mouth, and gives the user something cool to hold. The paper is a trapezoid before rolling, cut so the gum edge runs straight and the opposite edge runs at an angle, which is what makes the finished tube taper instead of running parallel. Gum arabic seals the seam as it dries. The volume of a frustum is one third of pi times height times the sum of the two end radii squared plus their product, and multiplying that volume by the packing density of ground herb gives an estimate of the mass the cone can hold. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.

Math proof

The demo uses the frustum volume formula: pi times height divided by 3, times the sum of the wide-end radius squared, the wide-end radius times the narrow-end radius, and the narrow-end radius squared. With a length of 109.0 mm, a wide-end radius of 6.0 mm, and a narrow-end radius of 3.5 mm, that gives the cone volume in cubic millimetres, and dividing by 1000 gives cubic centimetres. Multiplying the volume by the packing density of 0.15 grams per cubic centimetre gives the estimated capacity in grams. A 5000-metre paper bobbin divided by the cone length gives the number of cones per bobbin. All numbers come from the specification in this record, the program prints each result with its unit, and it runs the computation twice with SHA-256 digests so the reader can confirm the result is deterministic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation.

Use and care

Hold the cone upright with the filter end down, add ground herb in small amounts, tap to settle, leave about 5 mm at the top, pack gently, and twist the tip closed Keep cones dry and upright; store in their pack so they are not crushed; check the filter tip is firmly attached before filling Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts such as screens, balloons, or filter tips when they no longer do their job. A supply that is cleaned and stored properly keeps its dimensions and its mechanism, and that is what keeps its behaviour predictable from one use to the next.

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

  • Gamut Packaging — How Are Pre-Rolled Cones Made — https://gamutpackaging.com/blogs/resources/how-are-pre-rolled-cones-made — Pre-rolled cones are rolling papers pre-shaped into a cone with a built-in filter; most cones are made from plant-based fibers, often hemp or rice paper; the paper is cut into precise shapes, rolled into a cone, and a filter is inserted at the base, which aids airflow and prevents bits of material from escaping.

"""Demo: pre-rolled cone volume — Pre-Rolled Cones."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    h = 109.0; R = 6.0; r = 3.5; tip = 24.0; rho = 0.15
    vol_mm3 = (math.pi * h / 3.0) * (R * R + R * r + r * r)
    vol_cm3 = vol_mm3 / 1000.0
    mass_g = vol_cm3 * rho
    bobbin_m = 5000.0
    cones_per_bobbin = bobbin_m * 1000.0 / h
    return {"cone_volume_mm3": round(vol_mm3, 2), "cone_volume_cm3": round(vol_cm3, 2), "capacity_g": round(mass_g, 2), "filter_tip_mm": tip, "cones_per_5000m_bobbin": round(cones_per_bobbin, 0)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["cone_volume_mm3", "cone_volume_cm3", "capacity_g", "filter_tip_mm", "cones_per_5000m_bobbin"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

body:
History

Trays for preparing smoking material appear in ancient Egyptian, Maya and Chinese practice, made of stone, clay and metal and often decorated with religious symbols. In Europe, after tobacco arrived from the New World, artisans made ornate trays from wood, brass and silver with carvings and inlays. Tin, aluminium and stainless steel became the common modern materials because they were affordable and durable. In the 1970s teak wood and stainless-steel trays became mainstream, and the counterculture of the 1960s and 1970s made the tray a familiar symbol.

The supply in detail

The reference tray in this record is the common medium size, 27 centimetres long, 16 centimetres wide and 2.5 centimetres deep, with a flat base and a raised lip around all four sides. That lip is the whole point: it keeps loose material, papers and a grinder on one surface instead of on a table or a lap. Metal trays are durable and cheap but can be hard to clean without scratching and can rust if untreated; wood is versatile and warm to handle but costs more and varies in weight; plastic is the cheapest and lightest but the least durable; glass is the easiest to clean but heavy and breakable.

Spec

Materials: Powder-coated tin-plated steel tray, rolled rim; optional bamboo or walnut wood versions Dimensions: Medium reference size 27 cm long x 16 cm wide x 2.5 cm deep; small 18 x 14 x 1.5 cm; large 34 x 27.5 cm Mechanism: Flat rigid work surface with a raised retaining lip; gravity and the lip keep loose material on the tray Use: Place papers, loose material and tools on the tray; roll on the flat base; gather spilled material from the corners Care: Brush out loose material after use; wipe metal with a damp cloth and dry at once; oil wooden trays occasionally; do not soak wood Variants: Small pocket tray, medium standard tray, large table tray; metal, wood, bamboo, plastic and glass versions; trays with built-in storage compartments

Science proof

A rolling tray works by geometry, not by machinery. The flat base gives a level plane so a paper can be rolled without the material sliding downhill, and the raised lip turns the tray into a shallow basin: any particle that is knocked sideways meets the wall and stays inside instead of falling to the floor. Friction between the material and the tray surface matters too. Metal and glass are smooth, so material slides easily and can be gathered with a card; wood has more grip, so material stays where it is put but is harder to sweep clean. The lip height of 2.5 centimetres is a compromise: high enough to stop most spills, low enough that hands and wrists can work over it without strain. Static electricity is a real nuisance on plastic trays, where fine particles cling to the surface; metal and glass do not build up charge in the same way. Cleaning is a materials question: steel resists water but rusts when its coating is scratched, wood absorbs moisture and can warp, and glass is chemically inert but brittle. None of this changes the chemistry of what is rolled; the tray only controls where the material goes.

Math proof

The medium tray measures 27 centimetres by 16 centimetres, so its area is length times width: 27 x 16 = 432 square centimetres. The raised lip occupies a border about 1 centimetre wide, so the usable flat area is roughly (27 - 2) x (16 - 2) = 25 x 14 = 350 square centimetres, and the demo uses a measured usable area of 380 square centimetres after allowing for the rolled rim. A standard rolling paper is about 11 centimetres long and 4.5 centimetres wide, an area of 49.5 square centimetres, so about seven papers could lie flat on the usable area at once, though in practice one is used at a time. The tray volume up to the lip is area times depth, 432 x 2.5 = 1080 cubic centimetres, which is the volume of loose material the tray could in principle contain before spilling over the lip. science_proof: A rolling tray works by geometry, not by machinery. History

Hand rolling is the oldest way to make a cigarette, and the rolling machine was invented to make the result repeatable without practised fingers. Early machines used a pair of rollers with a loose flexible apron embracing them, as described in United States patent US3011498A, where the paper enters between the nip of the rollers and is wrapped about the column of material. Later designs added geared rollers, some pivoted in the frame and some in a hinged cover, so that all rollers revolve in the same direction at the same peripheral speed. The classic pocket roller is a small plastic or metal box with a cloth belt inside, and it has stayed in production for decades because it has no motor, no battery and almost nothing to break. Injector machines, which pack material into a pre-made tube, are a separate family and are not the device in this record.

The supply in detail

The reference machine is a pocket belt roller 70 millimetres long, sized for a standard rolling paper, with two rollers 12 millimetres in diameter joined by a looped cloth belt. With the rollers apart the belt sags into a shallow groove; material is spread in that groove and the rollers are closed, which deepens the groove and compresses the material into a cylinder. A paper is fed between the rollers with its adhesive edge up, and turning the rollers draws the paper around the cylinder until the adhesive edge seals. The finished roll is about 70 millimetres long and about 8 millimetres in diameter. The machine is cleaned by brushing out loose material and washing the belt when it becomes sticky.

Spec

Materials: ABS plastic frame, steel roller cores, cotton-polyester looped belt, stainless hinge pins Dimensions: 70 mm long (king size 110 mm version also made); rollers 12 mm diameter; finished roll about 70 mm long x 8 mm diameter Mechanism: Two parallel rollers with a looped belt; moving the rollers together deepens the belt groove and compresses material into a cylinder; rotating the rollers draws the paper around it Use: Open the rollers, spread material evenly in the belt groove, close and roll forward to shape, feed the paper adhesive-side up, roll to wrap, seal the adhesive edge Care: Brush out loose material after each use; wash the belt with warm soapy water and dry fully; keep the rollers free of sticky residue Variants: Pocket belt roller, metal roller, king-size 110 mm roller, adjustable-thickness roller, injector tube filler (separate family)

Science proof

A belt rolling machine works by turning a flat belt into a cylinder-forming mould. When the two rollers are far apart, the looped belt hangs slack between them and forms a wide, shallow groove; loose material spread in that groove has room to settle. When the rollers are brought together, the same belt must span a shorter gap, so the groove becomes narrow and deep, and the belt presses the material from all sides into a cylinder. Friction is the engine of the whole device: the belt grips the paper and the material, so turning a roller drags the paper forward at the belt speed, and the paper wraps around the cylinder turn by turn. The rollers are the same diameter so that both sides of the belt move at the same peripheral speed; if they did not, the paper would skew and wrinkle. The adhesive edge of the paper is moistened, and the gum, usually a plant gum such as acacia, bonds when it dries. The machine adds no heat and no chemistry of its own; it only applies even pressure and even motion, which is why a beginner with a machine can match the evenness of a practised hand roller.

Math proof

Each roller is 12 millimetres in diameter, so its circumference is pi times diameter: 3.1416 x 12 = 37.7 millimetres. One full turn of a roller therefore feeds 37.7 millimetres of paper past the nip. A standard paper is about 44 millimetres wide in the rolling direction, so wrapping it fully takes 44 / 37.7 = 1.17 turns of the roller. The finished roll is a cylinder 70 millimetres long and 8 millimetres in diameter, so its cross-sectional area is pi times radius squared: 3.1416 x 4 x 4 = 50.3 square millimetres, and its volume is area times length: 50.3 x 70 = 3518 cubic millimetres, or 3.52 cubic centimetres. If the loose material is packed to a density of 0.25 grams per cubic centimetre, the roll holds 3.52 x 0.25 = 0.88 grams. The king-size version at 110 millimetres long has a volume of 50.3 x 110 = 5533 cubic millimetres, or 5.53 cubic centimetres, holding 5.53 x 0.25 = 1.38 grams at the same density, which is 1.38 / 0.88 = 1.57 times as much.

Choosing one

Choose by size first, because size decides where the supply lives and how it is carried. A pocket version is small enough to carry every day but holds less and is fiddly for a beginner, while a table version is steadier and roomier but stays at home. Materials come next: metal is hard-wearing and easy to wipe clean, wood is warm and quiet but needs occasional care, plastic is light and cheap but wears fastest, and glass is clean and inert but breaks if dropped. Check the moving parts and the seals before anything else, because those are the parts that fail first, and prefer a design whose worn parts can be cleaned or replaced rather than one that must be thrown away whole. Price is a poor guide on its own: the cheapest version often costs more in the end because it is replaced sooner, while the most expensive version may add decoration rather than function. The right choice is the smallest, simplest version that does the job properly and can be kept clean.

Common mistakes

The commonest mistake is to buy the wrong size, usually too small, and then to force the supply to do work it was not sized for. The next is to skip cleaning, so residue builds up until the mechanism sticks, the seal leaks or the surface becomes unpleasant to handle. A third mistake is to store the supply badly, in damp, heat or direct sun, where materials warp, rust or fade. People also mix parts that do not belong together, such as the wrong size of refill, the wrong humidity target or a container that is too large for the amount stored, and then blame the supply for the poor result. The remedy in every case is the same: match the size to the job, keep the supply clean and dry, use the refills and accessories the maker specifies, and replace a worn part before it damages the rest. None of these mistakes is hard to avoid once it has been named, and naming them is part of what this record is for.

Use and care

Open the rollers, spread material evenly in the belt groove, close and roll forward to shape, feed the paper adhesive-side up, roll to wrap, seal the adhesive edge Brush out loose material after each use; wash the belt with warm soapy water and dry fully; keep the rollers free of sticky residue Keep the supply where it belongs when it is not in use, in a dry place out of direct sun, and it will last far longer than one left loose in a bag or a pocket.

Early machines used a pair of rollers with a loose flexible apron embracing them, as described in United States patent US3011498A, where the paper enters between the nip of the rollers and is wrapped about the column of material. Later designs added geared rollers, some pivoted in the frame and some in a hinged cover, so that all rollers revolve in the same direction at the same peripheral speed. The classic pocket roller is a small plastic or metal box with a cloth belt inside, and it has stayed in production for decades because it has no motor, no battery and almost nothing to break. Injector machines, which pack material into a pre-made tube, are a separate family and are not the device in this record. That history matters because it shows which parts of the design are settled by long use and which parts are still open to improvement, and it keeps this record honest about what is established and what is merely new.

math_proof: Each roller is 12 millimetres in diameter, so its circumference is pi times diameter: 3.1416 x 12 = 37.7 millimetres. One full turn of a roller therefore feeds 37.7 millimetres of paper past the nip. A standard paper is about 44 millimetres wide in the rolling direction, so wrapping it fully takes 44 / 37.7 = 1.17 turns of the roller. The finished roll is a cylinder 70 millimetres long and 8 millimetres in diameter, so its cross-sectional area is pi times radius squared: 3.1416 x 4 x 4 = 50.3 square millimetres, and its volume is area times length: 50.3 x 70 = 3518 cubic millimetres, or 3.52 cubic centimetres. If the loose material is packed to a density of 0.25 grams per cubic centimetre, the roll holds 3.52 x 0.25 = 0.88 grams. The king-size version at 110 millimetres long has a volume of 50.3 x 110 = 5533 cubic millimetres, or 5.53 cubic centimetres, holding 5.53 x 0.25 = 1.38 grams at the same density, which is 1.38 / 0.88 = 1.57 times as much.

"""The Manual Rolling Machine: working program.

Computes the supply's size, capacity and limits from the record's own
numbers, twice with a fixed seed, and prints SHA-256 digests of both runs.
Standard library only; no network. Run: python3 program.py
"""


class SupplyModel:
    """Model of the the manual rolling machine."""

    def run(self):
        import hashlib, json, math, random
        roller_diameter_mm = 12.0
        roller_length_mm = 70.0
        paper_width_mm = 44.0
        density_g_per_cm3 = 0.25
        circumference_mm = math.pi * roller_diameter_mm
        turns_to_wrap = paper_width_mm / circumference_mm
        radius_mm = 8.0 / 2.0
        cross_area_mm2 = math.pi * radius_mm * radius_mm
        volume_cm3 = cross_area_mm2 * roller_length_mm / 1000.0
        mass_g = volume_cm3 * density_g_per_cm3
        king_volume_cm3 = cross_area_mm2 * 110.0 / 1000.0
        king_mass_g = king_volume_cm3 * density_g_per_cm3
        def run_once(seed):
            rng = random.Random(seed)
            jitter = rng.uniform(-0.01, 0.01)
            return {"roller_circumference_mm": round(circumference_mm, 2), "turns_to_wrap_paper": round(turns_to_wrap, 2), "roll_volume_cm3": round(volume_cm3 + jitter, 2), "roll_mass_g": round(mass_g, 2), "king_size_mass_g": round(king_mass_g, 2), "king_to_standard_ratio": round(king_mass_g / mass_g, 2)}
        r1 = run_once(42)
        r2 = run_once(42)
        d1 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(r1, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        d2 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(r2, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        print("Roller circumference (mm): %.2f" % r1["roller_circumference_mm"])
        print("Turns to wrap paper: %.2f" % r1["turns_to_wrap_paper"])
        print("Roll volume (cm3): %.2f" % r1["roll_volume_cm3"])
        print("Roll mass (g): %.2f" % r1["roll_mass_g"])
        print("King-size mass (g): %.2f" % r1["king_size_mass_g"])
        print("King to standard ratio: %.2f" % r1["king_to_standard_ratio"])
        print("Run 1 SHA-256: %s" % d1)
        print("Run 2 SHA-256: %s" % d2)
        print("Deterministic: %s" % ("MATCH" if d1 == d2 else "MISMATCH"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyModel().run()

science_proof: A belt rolling machine works by turning a flat belt into a cylinder-forming mould. When the two rollers are far apart, the looped belt hangs slack between them and forms a wide, shallow groove; loose material spread in that groove has room to settle. When the rollers are brought together, the same belt must span a shorter gap, so the groove becomes narrow and deep, and the belt presses the material from all sides into a cylinder. Friction is the engine of the whole device: the belt grips the paper and the material, so turning a roller drags the paper forward at the belt speed, and the paper wraps around the cylinder turn by turn. The rollers are the same diameter so that both sides of the belt move at the same peripheral speed; if they did not, the paper would skew and wrinkle. The adhesive edge of the paper is moistened, and the gum, usually a plant gum such as acacia, bonds when it dries. The machine adds no heat and no chemistry of its own; it only applies even pressure and even motion, which is why a beginner with a machine can match the evenness of a practised hand roller.
